Formal.distortion: invalid inference wearing the costume of necessity.
Formal.danger: It gives a conclusion the feel of deductive force even when the structure does not license it.
Formal.user_action: Toggle premises as true or false, then try to make the conclusion false while the premises stay true.
Formal.feedback: If a possible world keeps the premises true while the conclusion fails, the app highlights the invalid step.

Mathematical.distortion: number-shaped confidence without proper numerical grounding.
Mathematical.danger: It makes quantities, probabilities, rates, or samples push confidence farther than the math permits.
Mathematical.user_action: Adjust sample size, base rate, comparison class, and uncertainty reserve to see how the apparent result changes.
Mathematical.feedback: The app shows how the conclusion shifts when the relevant denominator, base rate, or uncertainty is restored.

Causal.danger: It makes one causal pathway feel established before alternatives, confounders, and directionality are tested.
Causal.user_action: Draw the claimed causal path, then add confounders, reverse arrows, and rival explanations.
Causal.feedback: The app marks any unsupported causal arrow and shows which extra observations would discriminate among paths.

Linguistic.distortion: word movement disguised as argument movement.
Linguistic.danger: It lets ambiguity, framing, or unstable wording do work that evidence or valid inference should do.
Linguistic.user_action: Highlight key terms, lock their meanings, and see where the argument changes meaning midstream.
Linguistic.feedback: The app flags semantic drift, loaded phrasing, and category shifts that alter the conclusion without new evidence.

Conceptual.danger: It warps the conceptual map so that distinctions, boundaries, or levels of analysis mislead the inference.
Conceptual.user_action: Sort cases into categories, test edge cases, and see whether the proposed boundary remains stable.
Conceptual.feedback: The app exposes hidden category choices and shows how different but defensible classifications alter the conclusion.

Evidential.distortion: confidence moving faster than the evidence.
Evidential.danger: It overstates, understates, cherry-picks, or misallocates the force of evidence.
Evidential.user_action: Assign weight to each item of evidence, then compare the resulting confidence to what the evidence actually supports.
Evidential.feedback: The app displays the gap between warranted confidence and the confidence created by the fallacious move.

Perceptual.distortion: appearance being promoted to reality too quickly.
Perceptual.danger: It converts what seems obvious, vivid, or visually salient into a stronger claim than perception justifies.
Perceptual.user_action: Separate what is directly perceived from what is inferred, then rate the strength of the bridge between them.
Perceptual.feedback: The app shows which parts are observation, interpretation, and speculation.

Perspectival.distortion: a narrow vantage point pretending to be the whole terrain.
Perspectival.danger: It mistakes one standpoint, timeframe, or interpretive frame for a complete evidential view.
Perspectival.user_action: View the same claim from different timeframes, agents, cultures, incentives, and information positions.
Perspectival.feedback: The app shows what becomes visible or hidden when the perspective changes.

Epistemic.danger: It corrupts the calibration of belief, doubt, burden, uncertainty, or standards of evidence.
Epistemic.user_action: Set baseline confidence, update on evidence, and reserve uncertainty for unknowns or rival explanations.
Epistemic.feedback: The app compares the user's update to a more disciplined evidence-proportional update.

Tactical.danger: It moves attention away from the claim's evidential status and toward a pressure tactic, distraction, or rhetorical maneuver.
Tactical.user_action: Trace the original claim, identify the move that changed the topic, and restore the burdened question.
Tactical.feedback: The app marks the point where the discussion stopped tracking the truth of the original claim.

Emotional.distortion: feeling doing the work of evidence.
Emotional.danger: It lets fear, disgust, outrage, hope, shame, or loyalty produce a confidence shift not earned by evidence.
Emotional.user_action: Rate the emotional pull and the evidential force separately, then compare their effects on confidence.
Emotional.feedback: The app shows when emotional salience is being mistaken for evidential strength.

records.name: Absence of evidence fallacy
records.definition: Occurs when someone treats a failure to find expected evidence as if it counted for nothing against the claim, even in a context where the claim should leave detectable traces.
records.example: Multiple audits found no trace of the vote-flipping scheme, but that proves nothing; if the conspiracy were real, of course it would leave no evidence.
records.notes: Sometimes absence of evidence really is weak evidence, especially when the search tools are poor or the target is hard to detect. But when repeated investigation under the right conditions turns up nothing, that absence is itself evidence.

caseStudies.summary: After officials in Springfield, Ohio said there were no credible reports supporting the September 2024 rumor that Haitian immigrants were abducting and eating pets, some defenders treated the lack of evidence as irrelevant or as proof of a cover-up rather than as evidence against the rumor. The fallacy here is Absence of evidence fallacy: someone treats a failure to find expected evidence as if it counted for nothing against the claim, even in a context where the claim should leave detectable traces. That matters here because sometimes absence of evidence really is weak evidence, especially when the search tools are poor or the target is hard to detect. A better analysis would remember that when repeated investigation under the right conditions turns up nothing, that absence is itself evidence.

Claims of widespread noncitizen voting in 2024 often survived repeated audits and official reviews by insisting that the absence of supporting evidence was exactly what one should expect from a hidden scheme. The fallacy here is Absence of evidence fallacy: someone treats a failure to find expected evidence as if it counted for nothing against the claim, even in a context where the claim should leave detectable traces. That matters here because sometimes absence of evidence really is weak evidence, especially when the search tools are poor or the target is hard to detect. A better analysis would remember that when repeated investigation under the right conditions turns up nothing, that absence is itself evidence.

records.name: Abstraction denial
records.definition: Occurs when someone denies the reality or causal relevance of a higher-level pattern just because the pattern is realized through lower-level parts.
records.example: There is no such thing as inflation hurting families; there are only individual transactions between buyers and sellers.
records.notes: Abstract patterns can still be real and explanatory even when they depend on smaller physical or social components. Economies, institutions, languages, and ecosystems do not stop being real because they are made of people, words, or organisms.

That matters here because abstract patterns can still be real and explanatory even when they depend on smaller physical or social components. A better analysis would remember that economies, institutions, languages, and ecosystems do not stop being real because they are made of people, words, or organisms.

records.name: Abstraction fallacy
records.definition: Occurs when a model, law, or abstraction drawn from experience is treated as if it were a logically necessary rule that reality cannot ever depart from.
records.example: Moore's Law says computing power keeps doubling, so any slowdown would be impossible.
records.notes: Useful abstractions describe patterns with varying scope and durability. They are not automatically eternal, exceptionless constraints on what can happen.

That matters here because useful abstractions describe patterns with varying scope and durability. A better analysis would remember that they are not automatically eternal, exceptionless constraints on what can happen.

records.name: Ad hominem
records.definition: Occurs when someone treats an attack on a person's character, motives, class, or biography as if it were a refutation of that person's argument.
records.example: An economist presents data against a tariff proposal, and the reply is: 'Why listen to her? She is an Ivy League elitist who has never worked a real job.'
records.notes: Character can matter when credibility itself is at issue, such as fraud, conflicts of interest, or proven dishonesty. The fallacy appears when those personal facts are used instead of answering the actual reasons or evidence.

caseStudies.summary: AP reported that a PAC opposing Shreveport mayor Adrian Perkins used an AI-generated attack ad that put his face on a chastened student in a principal's office. The case is a clean example of vivid, emotionally loaded presentation doing persuasive work that policy argument still had to do for itself. The fallacy here is Ad hominem: someone treats an attack on a person's character, motives, class, or biography as if it were a refutation of that person's argument. That matters here because character can matter when credibility itself is at issue, such as fraud, conflicts of interest, or proven dishonesty. That is the exact slip in this case: those personal facts are used instead of answering the actual reasons or evidence.

records.name: Affirmative conclusion from a negative premise
records.definition: Occurs when a syllogism tries to draw a positive conclusion even though one of the premises is negative in a way that cannot support that conclusion.
records.example: This source is not anonymous. Anonymous sources are unreliable. Therefore this source is reliable.
records.notes: Ruling something out does not automatically place it into the positive category you want. 'Not bad' does not by itself mean 'good,' and 'not that' does not by itself mean 'this.'

caseStudies.summary: Tribal arguments often move from 'we are not them' and 'they are bad' to 'therefore we are trustworthy,' even though the conclusion has not been earned. The fallacy here is Affirmative conclusion from a negative premise: a syllogism tries to draw a positive conclusion even though one of the premises is negative in a way that cannot support that conclusion. That matters here because ruling something out does not automatically place it into the positive category you want. A better analysis would remember that 'Not bad' does not by itself mean 'good,' and 'not that' does not by itself mean 'this.'

records.name: Affirming a disjunct
records.definition: Occurs when someone treats an ordinary 'or' as if it were exclusive and concludes that one option must be false because the other is true.
records.example: This video is either edited or misleading. It is edited, so it cannot also be misleading.
records.notes: Some disjunctions are genuinely exclusive, but many are not. Two options can coexist unless the statement or context really rules that out.

caseStudies.summary: AP and NPR both showed how a few real or suspected ineligible votes were repeatedly used to argue that federal elections are broadly compromised. The jump from a narrow premise to a sweeping conclusion is exactly why formal discipline matters in public reasoning. The fallacy here is Affirming a disjunct: someone treats an ordinary 'or' as if it were exclusive and concludes that one option must be false because the other is true. That matters here because some disjunctions are genuinely exclusive, but many are not. A better analysis would remember that two options can coexist unless the statement or context really rules that out.

records.name: Affirming the consequent
records.definition: Occurs when someone reasons from 'if A, then B' and then wrongly infers A merely because B is observed.
records.example: If a clip is AI-generated, it may show warped hands. This clip shows warped hands, so it must be AI-generated.
records.notes: A consequence can have many causes. Observing the result does not tell you which sufficient condition produced it.

caseStudies.summary: AP's 2024 reporting on AI political content repeatedly showed how easy it is for people to move from 'this image has a common AI tell' to 'therefore this image must be AI-generated.' That conclusion can be tempting in practice, but the fact pattern only supports a possibility, not a guaranteed diagnosis. The fallacy here is Affirming the consequent: someone reasons from 'if A, then B' and then wrongly infers A merely because B is observed. That matters here because a consequence can have many causes. A better analysis would remember that observing the result does not tell you which sufficient condition produced it.

records.name: All or nothing fallacy
records.definition: Occurs when support for part of a view, or problems with part of a view, are treated as if they force total acceptance or total rejection of the whole package.
records.example: One error in this report means the entire investigation is worthless.
records.notes: Many systems of belief, institutions, and documents are mixed. Partial support or partial failure rarely justifies an everything-or-nothing verdict.

records.name: Exclusive premises
records.definition: Occurs when two negative premises are used in a syllogism even though they fail to establish the positive link the conclusion requires.

The fallacy here is Proof by verbosity: a claim is protected by an avalanche of words, side points, jargon, or branching assertions that overwhelm reasonable scrutiny and create the illusion of depth. That matters here because complexity is not itself a fallacy. A better analysis would remember that the problem is using sprawl as a shield, making it costly to respond point by point and then treating any unanswered fragment as proof of victory.

records.name: Wishful thinking
records.definition: Occurs when a belief or decision is driven mainly by what would be pleasing, hopeful, or comforting if true rather than by what the evidence supports.
records.example: This stock is too exciting to fail, so I am sure it will recover.
records.notes: Hope can sustain action, but it does not convert possibility into evidence. The stronger the desire, the easier it is to mistake wanting for warrant.

records.name: Witness chain
records.definition: Occurs when testimony is padded by unverifiable references to other alleged witnesses, creating the illusion of corroboration without actually providing independent support.
records.example: I saw the miracle myself, and dozens of others saw it too, though none of them are available to check.
records.notes: Real corroboration requires accessible, independent testimony or records. Simply claiming that more witnesses exist adds almost nothing if the chain cannot be examined.

caseStudies.summary: Paranormal, religious, and conspiracy stories often swell in authority by invoking unnamed doctors, secret insiders, or hundreds of silent observers who never become independently available. The fallacy here is Witness chain: testimony is padded by unverifiable references to other alleged witnesses, creating the illusion of corroboration without actually providing independent support. That matters here because real corroboration requires accessible, independent testimony or records. A better analysis would remember that simply claiming that more witnesses exist adds almost nothing if the chain cannot be examined.

records.name: Wrong causal direction
records.definition: Occurs when a real association is noticed but the direction of causation is reversed.
records.example: People who are already struggling concentrate more on self-help content, so the content must be what created the struggle.
records.notes: Correlations can be real while still pointing the wrong way. Without evidence about timing, mechanism, and alternatives, reversing cause and effect is easy.

caseStudies.summary: When AP covered Google's erroneous AI overviews, the central lesson was that a system can sound authoritative while still misreading queries, flattening context, or repeating bad source material. The episode is a strong real-world case of surface fluency masking evidential and conceptual weakness. The fallacy here is Wrong causal direction: a real association is noticed but the direction of causation is reversed. That matters here because correlations can be real while still pointing the wrong way. A better analysis would remember that without evidence about timing, mechanism, and alternatives, reversing cause and effect is easy.
